description.en-US: The sale this request serves. ONE ORDER HAS MANY REQUESTS (BR 45): partial delivery, several warehouses and split shipment each produce another, which is why this is a child table rather than a fulfillment_reference column on the order. A single column would have to be rewritten on the second shipment, losing the first.

What Sales is asking Inventory to do. INTENT, never instruction (BR 44): Sales says goods were sold and must leave, and Inventory decides availability, warehouse, location and the movements that follow. Immutable, because a request that changed its own kind would leave the movements it already caused unexplained.

How far Inventory has got. 'accepted' means the request was taken and stock reserved; 'completed' means the goods actually moved. The two are distinct because BR 7.3's failure - money captured but goods not dispensed - lives exactly between them, and a single 'done' flag could not express it.

Inventory's own identifier for whatever it created - a stock transfer id. A plain string with no foreign key: it points into another module, and a constraint across that boundary would make the two undeployable apart. Null until Inventory has accepted and told us what it made.
Why Inventory refused, in its own words. Kept because a rejected fulfilment is the case an operator has to act on, and 'rejected' alone tells them nothing about whether to wait, re-route or refund.
When the goods actually moved. Null until then, including while the request is merely accepted - see the note on status.
